challenges.opponent_argument: The standing theory overreads R.C. 5301.07. The statute creates only a rebuttable presumption about a recorded instrument; it does not itself adjudicate marketable title or automatically confer standing to sue. The brief’s own timeline shows the corrective affidavit was not recorded until October 10, 2017, after the July 6, 2017 complaint, so Appellee was relying on a deed that still needed a later cure. Ohio quiet-title law turns on a present property interest, and the authority the brief cites does not say a defect plus a later affidavit retroactively creates standing at filing.
challenges.why_it_matters: If standing was absent when suit began, the quiet-title and related claims were subject to dismissal regardless of what happened later.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a live appellate attack, but it does not cleanly defeat the brief on this record. The cited statute does create only a rebuttable presumption, so opposing counsel is right that R.C. 5301.07 by itself does not literally say "standing." But the brief already answers the timing point: it says the sheriff's deed was recorded on May 16, 2017, the complaint was filed July 6, 2017, standing is measured at commencement, and the deed was presumed valid absent fraud/forgery-type proof. The later corrective affidavit is not the sole pillar of the standing argument. The advocate stands to lose Assignment I only if the court holds the recorded deed with the clerical defect conveyed no enforceable interest at filing.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee had standing when it filed suit because it already held a recorded sheriff’s deed to the Property. R.C. 5301.07(B)(1) created a rebuttable presumption that the recorded deed was valid, enforceable, and effective, and Appellant identified no clear-and-convincing evidence of fraud, undue influence, duress, forgery, incompetency, or incapacity under R.C. 5301.07(B)(2). The later affidavit merely corrected the scrivener’s error in the notary block; it did not create Appellee’s interest, which existed when the deed was recorded on May 16, 2017, well before the Complaint was filed on July 6, 2017.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tighten the standing argument so it does not sound as if R.C. 5301.07 alone confers standing. Focus on the recorded sheriff’s deed, the statutory presumption of validity for a recorded real-property instrument, and the absence of any record evidence rebutting that presumption.

challenges.opponent_argument: The fraud summary-judgment theory is missing the reliance element. Fraud requires a false material representation, justifiable reliance, and resulting injury. The brief never identifies any representation that Appellee relied on when it acquired the property or filed suit; instead, it says Appellee had no knowledge of Appellants’ work until after acquisition, which cuts against reliance rather than proving it. A false recorded lien may be evidence of falsity, but it is not fraud absent transactional reliance and causation.
challenges.why_it_matters: Without reliance, the fraud count cannot stand as a matter of law, so summary judgment on that claim should not be affirmed.

challenges.judge_assessment: This lands harder. Fraud in Ohio still requires reliance and causation, and the brief's own record is thin on who relied on what false statement when Appellee bought the property or filed suit. The brief tries to reframe the "transaction" as the transfer of title and the public recording of the liens, but that is not a full answer to the reliance element. Saying Appellee lacked knowledge until after acquisition cuts against, rather than supports, traditional fraud reliance. If the court accepts this attack, the fraud count should not have been resolved for Appellee as a matter of law.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee submitted evidence that Appellants recorded three mechanic’s-lien affidavits containing false statements that Appellants had contracts and were owed money, that Appellants knew those statements were false, and that the filings were made to mislead others and interfere with Appellee’s title and use of the Property. Appellants filed no timely evidentiary opposition and offered no competing proof on summary judgment. On this record, the trial court properly concluded that no genuine issue of material fact remained as to Appellants’ fraudulent conduct. At a minimum, any dispute Appellant raises about the fraud theory does not defeat the separate summary judgment entered on slander of title.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the fraud discussion. If the record does not give you a clean citation to reliance, do not overstate that element; instead emphasize the knowingly false recorded affidavits, Appellants’ intent to mislead, the absence of a timely evidentiary opposition, and, if necessary, argue that any weakness in the fraud analysis does not disturb the separate slander-of-title ruling.

challenges.opponent_argument: The slander-of-title theory is also incomplete. The brief cites the existence of allegedly false mechanic’s liens and the absence of contracts, but slander of title requires malicious falsity and pecuniary loss. The motion papers described here do not show competent evidence of a concrete, non-speculative loss caused by the filings, and the late opposition does not relieve Appellee of its Dresher burden to prove every element with admissible evidence.
challenges.why_it_matters: If malice or pecuniary loss was not established as a matter of law, summary judgment on slander of title was premature.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a substantial vulnerability, though not as sharp as the fraud attack. Slander of title requires malicious falsity and pecuniary loss. The brief points to false lien filings, recklessness, and damages 'expected,' but that is not the same thing as a concrete, admissible showing of special damages caused by the filings. The later jury trial on damages helps the appellee somewhat, yet it does not fully cure a weak summary-judgment record on the elements of the tort. If the court views the summary-judgment evidence as only speculative on loss, this claim is exposed.
challenges.suggested_response: Slander of title requires malicious falsity and pecuniary loss, but at the summary-judgment stage Appellee was not required to prove the final amount of damages. Civ.R. 56(C) expressly permits summary judgment on liability alone even where the amount of damages remains for later determination. Here, Appellee presented evidence that Appellants filed false mechanic’s liens on the Property, that Appellants lacked contracts to support at least two of those filings, that the filings were made in reckless disregard of Appellee’s rights, and that damages were reasonably expected as a result. The jury later determined the amount of compensatory damages. The trial court therefore properly entered summary judgment on the slander-of-title claim.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Answer this by distinguishing liability from the amount of damages. Emphasize that Civ.R. 56(C) permits summary judgment on liability alone and that the summary-judgment record showed false liens, lack of contract support, and expected damages, while the precise amount was later tried.

challenges.opponent_argument: The punitive-damages submission rests too heavily on Appellant Woods’s courtroom demeanor in the second phase of trial. Actual malice has to be shown in connection with the underlying wrongful conduct, not just by pointing to hostile or combative behavior at trial after liability has already been decided. The brief never ties that demeanor to the filing of the liens themselves, so the malice predicate is thin even if the punitive-to-compensatory ratio is not facially extreme.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the malice finding was unsupported, the punitive-damages instruction and award cannot stand regardless of the amount.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack has some bite, but it overstates the record problem. The brief does lean on Woods's hostile conduct during the punitive phase, which by itself is not the cleanest way to prove actual malice for punitive damages. But the brief also ties punitive damages to the underlying false lien filings, the fraud verdict, and testimony the jury heard in both phases. Because the court had already denied a directed verdict and no objection was made to the instructions, this is not an easy reversal point on this record. The advocate mainly risks losing the punitive award, not the whole case.
challenges.suggested_response: Punitive damages were proper because the jury heard evidence of Appellants’ underlying malicious conduct in recording false lien affidavits and interfering with Appellee’s title, and that conduct supported a finding of actual malice. Woods’s hostile and combative conduct during the second phase of trial was additional evidence of ill will; it was not the sole basis for punitive damages. Appellants did not object to the final punitive-damages instructions, and the trial court denied their motion for directed verdict on that issue. The punitive award bore a rational relationship to the compensatory award and was not the product of passion or prejudice.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the least persuasive attack as framed. The brief does not rely only on mootness; it also argues lis pendens attached before the liens, the liens were filed after the lis pendens date, and later release of the liens meant the challenge to the 12(C) order was moot or waived. Opposing counsel is right that a later release does not prove the July 17, 2019 ruling was correct on the merits, but that point alone does not defeat the brief because the underlying lis pendens argument is separately stated. On this record, the appellate court is more likely to look past the waiver rhetoric and decide whether the pleadings and dates supported judgment.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellee does not rely on the later release of the liens to prove the correctness of the Civ.R. 12(C) ruling. The ruling was correct on the pleadings because the foreclosure complaint was filed before Appellants recorded the mechanic’s liens, and lis pendens charged later claimants with notice of the pending action and subjecting any later-acquired interest to the outcome of that litigation. The later release of the liens simply confirms that Appellants did not obtain a stay and did not preserve any live controversy over enforcement of the order; it does not supply the merits, which are established by the dates alleged and admitted in the pleadings.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not lean on mootness alone. Make the merits point under lis pendens and the complaint-and-lien dates, and use the later release only as a separate point that Appellants did not stay or appeal enforcement of the 12(C) order.

attacks_proposed.argument: The standing theory overreads R.C. 5301.07. The statute creates only a rebuttable presumption about a recorded instrument; it does not itself adjudicate marketable title or automatically confer standing to sue. The brief’s own timeline shows the corrective affidavit was not recorded until October 10, 2017, after the July 6, 2017 complaint, so Appellee was relying on a deed that still needed a later cure. Ohio quiet-title law turns on a present property interest, and the authority the brief cites does not say a defect plus a later affidavit retroactively creates standing at filing.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If standing was absent when suit began, the quiet-title and related claims were subject to dismissal regardless of what happened later.

attacks_proposed.argument: The mootness/waiver discussion does not answer whether the judgment on the pleadings was correct when entered. Appellee relies on later lien release and the absence of a stay, but that is not the same as showing the July 17, 2019 Civ.R. 12(C) ruling was legally sound at the time it was made. A later enforcement step by the prevailing party cannot retroactively supply the missing elements of a pleadings-stage quiet-title claim.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the appellate court reviews the 12(C) ruling on its merits, the later release of the liens does not insulate an erroneous judgment from reversal.

attacks_proposed.argument: The fraud summary-judgment theory is missing the reliance element. Fraud requires a false material representation, justifiable reliance, and resulting injury. The brief never identifies any representation that Appellee relied on when it acquired the property or filed suit; instead, it says Appellee had no knowledge of Appellants’ work until after acquisition, which cuts against reliance rather than proving it. A false recorded lien may be evidence of falsity, but it is not fraud absent transactional reliance and causation.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without reliance, the fraud count cannot stand as a matter of law, so summary judgment on that claim should not be affirmed.

attacks_proposed.argument: The slander-of-title theory is also incomplete. The brief cites the existence of allegedly false mechanic’s liens and the absence of contracts, but slander of title requires malicious falsity and pecuniary loss. The motion papers described here do not show competent evidence of a concrete, non-speculative loss caused by the filings, and the late opposition does not relieve Appellee of its Dresher burden to prove every element with admissible evidence.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If malice or pecuniary loss was not established as a matter of law, summary judgment on slander of title was premature.

attacks_proposed.argument: The punitive-damages submission rests too heavily on Appellant Woods’s courtroom demeanor in the second phase of trial. Actual malice has to be shown in connection with the underlying wrongful conduct, not just by pointing to hostile or combative behavior at trial after liability has already been decided. The brief never ties that demeanor to the filing of the liens themselves, so the malice predicate is thin even if the punitive-to-compensatory ratio is not facially extreme.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the malice finding was unsupported, the punitive-damages instruction and award cannot stand regardless of the amount.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a live appellate attack, but it does not cleanly defeat the brief on this record. The cited statute does create only a rebuttable presumption, so opposing counsel is right that R.C. 5301.07 by itself does not literally say "standing." But the brief already answers the timing point: it says the sheriff's deed was recorded on May 16, 2017, the complaint was filed July 6, 2017, standing is measured at commencement, and the deed was presumed valid absent fraud/forgery-type proof. The later corrective affidavit is not the sole pillar of the standing argument. The advocate stands to lose Assignment I only if the court holds the recorded deed with the clerical defect conveyed no enforceable interest at filing.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: Recorded sheriff's deed on May 16 created a rebuttable presumption of a valid, enforceable, effective instrument; standing is measured at filing; no fraud, forgery, duress, incompetency, or incapacity was shown.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio authority on whether a recorder-accepted sheriff's deed with a scrivener's error conveys an enforceable interest before corrective affidavit; whether 5301.07 or 2329.31 governs sheriff's deeds specifically.

judge_assessments.assessment: This lands harder. Fraud in Ohio still requires reliance and causation, and the brief's own record is thin on who relied on what false statement when Appellee bought the property or filed suit. The brief tries to reframe the "transaction" as the transfer of title and the public recording of the liens, but that is not a full answer to the reliance element. Saying Appellee lacked knowledge until after acquisition cuts against, rather than supports, traditional fraud reliance. If the court accepts this attack, the fraud count should not have been resolved for Appellee as a matter of law.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It says the false mechanic's liens were recorded, Appellants knew the statements were false, intended to mislead, and Appellee showed justifiable reliance and damages expected; it also says Appellants filed no timely opposing evidence.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio cases on whether recording a false lien can satisfy fraud's reliance element, and whether reliance by a title holder or third parties suffices absent a purchase or transactional reliance by the plaintiff.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is a substantial vulnerability, though not as sharp as the fraud attack. Slander of title requires malicious falsity and pecuniary loss. The brief points to false lien filings, recklessness, and damages 'expected,' but that is not the same thing as a concrete, admissible showing of special damages caused by the filings. The later jury trial on damages helps the appellee somewhat, yet it does not fully cure a weak summary-judgment record on the elements of the tort. If the court views the summary-judgment evidence as only speculative on loss, this claim is exposed.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: It relies on the false recorded liens, admissions that no contracts existed for two of them, recklessness/wanton conduct, and the assertion that damages were expected and later quantified at trial.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Ohio slander-of-title authority on what counts as special damages/pecuniary loss at summary judgment, and whether a later damages trial can cure an element-specific deficiency on the liability ruling.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack has some bite, but it overstates the record problem. The brief does lean on Woods's hostile conduct during the punitive phase, which by itself is not the cleanest way to prove actual malice for punitive damages. But the brief also ties punitive damages to the underlying false lien filings, the fraud verdict, and testimony the jury heard in both phases. Because the court had already denied a directed verdict and no objection was made to the instructions, this is not an easy reversal point on this record. The advocate mainly risks losing the punitive award, not the whole case.

results.assessment: The brief has some solid footing on standing and the later procedural issues: the recorded deed timing and the lis pendens/waiver argument give it a plausible path. But the most serious weaknesses are the missing fraud reliance element and the thin slander-of-title proof of concrete, admissible pecuniary loss; those are the places an opponent can most effectively attack the summary-judgment record. Punitive damages are also somewhat vulnerable because the briefing leans too much on trial demeanor, though that point is less likely to undo the whole case. challenges.opponent_argument: The standing theory leans on the wrong statute. R.C. 5301.07 is a curative provision for "real property instruments," but the authorities actually governing sheriff's-sale conveyances are R.C. 2329.31 and 2329.36. Source 6 requires the court to examine whether the judicial sale conformed to the foreclosure statutes, and source 8 separately prescribes the contents of a sheriff's deed. The brief never explains why a notary-block scrivener's error in a sheriff's deed automatically receives the same presumption as an ordinary acknowledged deed under 5301.07. Without that statutory fit, recording plus a later corrective affidavit does not establish enforceable title or standing.
challenges.why_it_matters: If 5301.07 does not apply the way the brief says, appellee had not shown a valid property interest when suit was filed, and the standing ruling falls.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real appellate pressure point, but it is not as clean as the attack suggests. Ohio fraud requires reliance and injury, and the brief does more than cite the elements: it points to recorded lien affidavits, admissions that several claimed contracts did not exist, and discovery responses allegedly showing knowledge the statements were false. challenges.suggested_response: Appellee’s summary-judgment evidence showed that appellants recorded mechanic’s-lien affidavits containing false statements about nonexistent contracts and amounts allegedly owed, and that appellants knew those statements were false. Under the authorities cited in the brief, a recorded mechanic’s lien may support a fraud claim where the filer knew the statements were false, and slander of title is established by the wrongful recording of an unfounded claim that causes pecuniary loss. challenges.judge_assessment: This attack has force because punitive damages in Ohio require actual malice, and malice must be tied to the underlying tortious conduct, not merely to bad courtroom behavior. The brief does not fully separate those concepts; it leans on the false lien filings, the fraud/slander findings, and Woods’s hostile conduct at the punitive phase. Hostility in court is not by itself enough. Still, the brief does not rest only on demeanor: it invokes the false filings, the jury’s liability findings, the directed-verdict ruling, and the lack of objection to the instructions. So this is a substantial but answerable challenge, not an obvious reversal on the face of the brief.
challenges.suggested_response: Punitive damages were properly submitted because appellee presented evidence from which the jury could find actual malice in appellants’ conduct when they recorded false mechanic’s-lien affidavits against appellee’s Property. The evidence showed that appellants knew the statements in the liens were false, yet filed them to assert an unfounded claim and obtain payment. That conduct permitted the jury to find a conscious disregard of appellee’s rights and a great probability of substantial harm. Woods’s conduct during the punitive-damages phase further corroborated the malice the jury was entitled to infer from the underlying filings. Appellants also failed to object to the final punitive-damages instructions, and the jury’s award was not so disproportionate as to show passion or prejudice.

Their challenge to the punitive-damages instructions fails because they did not object to the final instructions, and they therefore waived any claim of instructional error. results.assessment: The brief has a workable overall narrative and it does answer some attacks with statutory text, the recorded deed, and waiver-oriented responses. But its most vulnerable points are clear: it leans on the wrong statutory frame for standing without fully explaining why a sheriff’s-deed notary-block defect is cured the way an ordinary deed would be; it is thin on record-specific proof for fraud and slander of title because the reliance/causation chain is not well developed; and punitive damages are not cleanly tied to actual malice at the time of the liens rather than to courtroom conduct. The 12(C) and JNOV/new-trial sections are more defensible, but they mostly track the same weaknesses rather than fix them.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. The cited authority supports apparent authority as a doctrine that binds a principal to an agent's act, not as a device for an actor to validate his own self-protective release. The brief actually concedes that point in part, then tries to repurpose apparent authority and estoppel against Lundberg himself. On this record, that is a real doctrinal mismatch. The brief does not fully answer it; it relies on Kevin Sheridan's testimony and the signed release, but that still does not supply the missing principal-side manifestation or ratification from Equity Trust. The point is narrower: Eric Lundberg signed a written Release of Lien, gave the original to Kevin Sheridan, and participated in an arrangement under which the loan would be repaid by other means and he would be left as an unsecured creditor. Whatever label is attached to that arrangement, those facts show that Lundberg cannot now claim a compensable injury from Land Title’s accommodation filing. At a minimum, he is estopped from denying the effect of the release he executed and delivered.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real vulnerability, but it does not fully defeat the brief on its own. The authority cited for causation does not prove that a signed document alone conclusively extinguishes the lien, and the release text itself creates a tension the brief never squarely resolves: it names Equity Trust as the undersigned owner/holder while the brief simultaneously argues Lundberg individually signed it and also that only Equity Trust could release the mortgage. The brief does answer part of the attack by emphasizing the signed, witnessed, notarized release, the delivery of the original, and the parties' intent to convert the debt into an unsecured arrangement. But if the court treats the identity/authority mismatch as fatal, Land Title loses the cleanest path to saying the injury had already been eliminated.
challenges.suggested_response: The relevant point is not a technical dispute over labels in the instrument; it is that Eric Lundberg signed and delivered a written Release of Lien that, on its face, released the lien described by instrument number 200702201238. Kevin Sheridan testified that he received the release from Eric Lundberg and that the parties made other arrangements to repay the loan. On that record, Land Title’s accommodation filing did not create the injury Appellant claims, because Lundberg had already agreed to relinquish the security interest and proceed as an unsecured creditor.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not try to make the release theory turn on a perfect reconciliation of the mortgagee name and Lundberg’s signature. Recast the point as one about Lundberg’s own execution and delivery of the release, plus the parties’ understood change in repayment arrangement, which defeats any claimed injury from the accommodation filing.

challenges.opponent_argument: The brief does not prove the release was actually effective in the real world; it only shows a signed paper existed. Land Title says the release “could have been filed at any time” if someone had the original (u71), and Kevin Sheridan’s testimony is that he received the document, later gave it to Christine, and did not know what was ultimately done with it (u73, u256, u260). Land Title also describes the whole setup as a device to make the property look over-encumbered (u128, u239, u263). That is a factual dispute about whether the document was intended to operate as an immediate discharge, not proof of a completed release.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the release was not shown to have been operative, Land Title cannot use it to erase damages as a matter of law.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack is mostly a factual reframing of a2. The brief does not claim there was a recorded release; instead it says the signed release existed, could have been filed, was delivered, and reflected the parties' intended restructuring. That is enough for the brief's causation theory even if the document was never actually recorded. The attack would need Ohio authority showing that lack of filing prevented the release from having legal effect relevant to damages. No such authority is supplied here. On this record, the court is unlikely to treat the absence of proof that someone later recorded it as defeating summary judgment by itself.
challenges.suggested_response: Appellant’s contention that the release was never recorded does not defeat summary judgment on causation. Land Title’s point is not that a later filing is shown in the record; it is that Eric Lundberg executed a written Release of Lien, gave the original to Kevin Sheridan, and understood that the loan would be repaid through other arrangements rather than by enforcing the mortgage against the Sheridan home. Whether someone later filed the document is not the fact that controls injury here. The record shows that Lundberg voluntarily agreed to become an unsecured creditor, so Land Title’s accommodation filing was not the proximate cause of any claimed loss.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow the argument away from whether the release was later recorded and toward the fact that the signed release existed, was delivered, and reflected the parties’ intended unsecured arrangement. Make clear that the absence of proof about later recording does not create a material causation dispute on this record.

attacks_proposed.argument: Summary judgment cannot be affirmed on a record that the brief itself says contains disputed facts. Land Title repeatedly claims the material facts are undisputed (u21, u285), but the same brief concedes factual disputes over who signed the mortgage, what authority existed, and whether the release was operative (u133, u137, u198). Under the Civ.R. 56 standard, the court may not resolve those disputes in Land Title’s favor; it must construe them for the nonmovant.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If genuine disputes remain on the predicates to causation and authority, summary judgment has to fall.

attacks_proposed.argument: Land Title’s release theory is internally inconsistent. The release text says the undersigned is Equity Trust Company, Custodian FBO Eric Lundberg IRA #49550, the present legal and equitable owner and holder (u45, u46, u196), yet the brief also insists Lundberg personally was not the mortgagee and that only Equity Trust could release the mortgage (u151, u156, u159). If Lundberg lacked title or authority, his signature alone cannot be treated as conclusively extinguishing the lien. That breaks the chain Land Title needs to eliminate causation.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without an operative release by the actual holder, Land Title cannot say the alleged injury was already gone before its filing.

attacks_proposed.argument: The brief does not prove the release was actually effective in the real world; it only shows a signed paper existed. Land Title says the release “could have been filed at any time” if someone had the original (u71), and Kevin Sheridan’s testimony is that he received the document, later gave it to Christine, and did not know what was ultimately done with it (u73, u256, u260). Land Title also describes the whole setup as a device to make the property look over-encumbered (u128, u239, u263). That is a factual dispute about whether the document was intended to operate as an immediate discharge, not proof of a completed release.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the release was not shown to have been operative, Land Title cannot use it to erase damages as a matter of law.

attacks_proposed.argument: The standing argument overreaches. The brief says Lundberg sued individually and as beneficial owner of the IRA held by Equity Trust (u173, u174), so he is not simply a stranger to the transaction. The brief also admits no assignment or power of attorney from Equity Trust was produced (u175), which means the ownership-and-authority question is unresolved, not that Lundberg necessarily lacks standing as a matter of law. At most, the record shows a disputed real-party-in-interest issue; it does not conclusively establish that only Equity Trust could sue.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the court accepts this as a categorical standing bar, it wrongly disposes of the merits without proof that Lundberg had no enforceable interest at all.

attacks_proposed.argument: The apparent-authority fallback fails on its own terms. The brief concedes that apparent authority is a principal-side doctrine, not a defense for the actor who signed the document (u184). Equity Trust—the only entity the brief says held the mortgage—is not a party and has not appeared to ratify anything (u170, u171, u175, u184). So Land Title cannot invoke apparent authority to convert Lundberg’s disputed personal execution into a binding release without a principal’s manifestation or ratification.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This knocks out the alternative basis for affirmance and leaves Land Title with no clean authority theory to sustain summary judgment.

attacks_proposed.argument: Land Title’s “no proximate cause” framing assumes the very point in dispute: that Lundberg would be in the same position even if the mortgage had not been filed or had been filed differently. But the brief’s own proximate-cause discussion turns on contested predicates—who held the mortgage, whether the release was operative, and what the parties intended (u11, u13, u143, u285). Source 41 recognizes proximate causation as a question of reasonable connection, and those connections cannot be adjudged as absent when the underlying facts remain contested.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If proximate cause depends on disputed predicate facts, the court cannot affirm on a blanket no-causation rationale across all tort theories.

judge_assessments.assessment: This is the strongest attack. The cited authority supports apparent authority as a doctrine that binds a principal to an agent's act, not as a device for an actor to validate his own self-protective release. The brief actually concedes that point in part, then tries to repurpose apparent authority and estoppel against Lundberg himself. On this record, that is a real doctrinal mismatch. The brief does not fully answer it; it relies on Kevin Sheridan's testimony and the signed release, but that still does not supply the missing principal-side manifestation or ratification from Equity Trust. Land Title stands to lose the alternative release/authority ground if the court reads the doctrine strictly.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief concedes apparent authority is usually principal-side, but argues that if Lundberg could enforce the mortgage he could also release it, and that Kevin Sheridan's words and conduct, together with the signed release, bound Lundberg by apparent authority or estoppel.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Further research on Ohio apparent authority and estoppel when the alleged actor is not the principal, and whether a custodian/IRA holder's signature can bind the underlying mortgage interest without ratification.

judge_assessments.assessment: This attack has some force because the standing cases cited by the brief establish the general requirement of standing, but they do not by themselves prove that naming Equity Trust as mortgagee automatically strips Lundberg of standing. The brief's logic is binary: if Equity Trust owns the mortgage, Lundberg lacks standing. That is not fully established on this record, especially given that the brief also says Lundberg sued individually and as beneficial owner of the IRA. The brief partially answers the point by asserting no assignment or power of attorney was produced and by framing the issue as Lundberg's own prior position, but the leap from 'custodian named on the mortgage' to 'no standing as a matter of law' is still contestable. Land Title risks losing the alternative no-standing ground, though not necessarily the whole judgment if proximate cause stands.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief says Lundberg argued below that Equity Trust, not Eric Lundberg, held the mortgage; therefore only Equity Trust could sue or release it. It adds that no assignment or power of attorney was produced and that Equity Trust is not a party.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Further research on Ohio real-party-in-interest doctrine for IRA custodial mortgages and whether a beneficial owner may sue or enforce where the custodian is named on the mortgage.

judge_assessments.assessment: Source 35 supports the ordinary Civ.R. 56 rule, so the general point is right: a court cannot grant summary judgment by resolving genuine material disputes against the nonmovant. But the brief already answers this by saying factual disputes exist yet are not material to proximate cause, and by anchoring its motion on an undisputed release and the parties' expectations. On this record, the attack only lands if the disputed issues over who signed what, what authority existed, or whether the release was operative are material to causation. If the court accepts the brief's framing, this attack does not defeat affirmance.
judge_assessments.briefCurrentlySays: The brief expressly says facts material to proximate cause are not in dispute, and later acknowledges some issues of fact exist but are not material to the analysis before the court.
judge_assessments.coverageNote: Further research would only matter if one needed to decide whether the release's validity and the parties' authority are material facts under Ohio summary judgment law in this mortgage-release context.

judge_assessments.assessment: This overlaps heavily with a1. Source 41 supports that proximate cause requires a reasonable connection, but it does not say disputed predicate facts automatically bar summary judgment. The brief already addresses this by arguing that, even assuming some disputes, Lundberg would be in the same position because he signed the release and expected to be an unsecured creditor. So the attack is not a knockout. It does have a real point if the court thinks the release was not operative or the parties' expectations were genuinely disputed in a way that changes the injury analysis. On the present brief, though, Land Title has already tried to close that gap.

results.verdict: reasonably persuasive on causation, but exposed on the autho
results.assessment: The brief has a workable summary-judgment and proximate-cause story, especially its emphasis on the signed release, delivery, and the claim that Lundberg expected to be an unsecured creditor. But it is vulnerable where it tries to turn that into a clean legal win: the apparent-authority fallback does not fit well because it lacks a principal-side manifestation or ratification, the standing argument overreaches on this record, and the release theory is internally strained by the mismatch between the named owner/holder and Lundberg’s individual execution. The research did not settle whether the lack of recording matters, but it does not by itself rescue the brief from the authority gap.

target.excerpt: The accommodation filing 3 of the Lundberg Mortgage by Land Title was not the proximate cause of Lundberg's alleged injuries and damages. The trial court properly concluded that based upon the undisputed facts of this case, proximate cause of injury cannot be shown.

challenges.judge_assessment: This does not seriously move the court on this record. Land Title’s brief already addresses the causation gap by tying Lundberg’s claimed position to the signed Release of Lien and the parties’ stated plan that he would be an unsecured creditor. It also argues that, even if the release was never recorded, Lundberg was in no worse position than he expected to be in. On this record, Land Title’s later filing did not change Lundberg’s bargain or place him in any different position than the one he expected when he executed the Release.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tighten the causation section so it says the claimed injury does not arise from Land Title’s filing step at all, because Lundberg had already signed and delivered the Release and expected to be an unsecured creditor. target.excerpt: 2.  APPELLANT LUNDBERG CANNOT HAVE IT BOTH WAYS-IF HE DOES NOT HAVE THE AUTHORITY TO RELEASE THE LIEN AT ISSUE, AS HE CLAIMS, THEN HE ALSO DOES NOT HAVE THE AUTHORITY (STANDING) TO ENFORCE IT.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack on the brief’s alternative standing theory. The brief does cite standing and real-party-in-interest cases, but it never cleanly bridges the gap between ‘Lundberg says only Equity Trust could release the mortgage’ and ‘therefore Lundberg himself lacks standing to sue for damages caused by Land Title.’ Those are different questions. challenges.suggested_response: Lundberg has not shown that he is the proper party to enforce rights under the mortgage. To the extent Lundberg’s claims depend on enforcing the mortgage interest itself, he has not carried his burden to show that he is the real party in interest entitled to assert those rights.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow this section. The brief should not claim that Lundberg’s asserted lack of authority to release the lien automatically means he lacks standing to sue all claims against Land Title. At most, on the record supplied, the better point is that he has not shown he is the proper party to enforce mortgage rights that the mortgage names in Equity Trust.

challenges.opponent_argument: The apparent-authority theory is unsupported because the brief never identifies a manifestation by the supposed principal, Equity Trust. Under the rule the brief quotes from Master Consolid. Corp. and Miller, apparent authority depends on the principal’s words or conduct causing the other party to believe authority exists. But the facts the brief cites are only Eric’s delivery of the release and Kevin Sheridan’s subjective understanding. target.excerpt: 3. ALTERNATIVELY, IF APPELLANT LUNDBERG HAS STANDING TO ENFORCE THE MORTGAGE LIEN, THEN HE ALSO HAD THE AUTHORITY TO RELEASE IT; HE CANNOT HAVE IT BOTH WAYS SIMPLY BECAUSE ONE ARGUMENT BENEFITS HIM AND THE OTHER HURTS HIM.

challenges.opponent_argument: The sanctions/vexatious-litigator request is unsupported by the materials provided. The brief recites a list of filings in different forums and then leaps to the conclusion that those filings satisfy R.C. 2323.52, but no record is supplied showing the substance of each filing, why each was frivolous or harassing, or the factual basis for the required statutory findings. A bare catalogue of case captions is not a substitute for the record a court needs to impose the extraordinary remedy the brief seeks.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the statutory findings are not supported by a developed record, the request to reverse the denial of sanctions and declare appellant a vexatious litigator cannot be sustained.

target.excerpt: V. THE TRIAL COURT ERRED IN FAILING TO GRANT DEFENDANT'S MOTION FOR SANCTIONS, WHICH INCLUDED DECLARING PLAINTIFF, WILFRED LOUIS ANDERSON, A VEXATIOUS LITIGATOR AS THAT TERM IS DEFINED IN OHIO REVISED CODE SECTION 2323.52 .

challenges.judge_assessment: R.C. 2323.52 does not let a party win by listing many cases alone; the statute turns on repeated vexatious conduct, lack of good-faith basis, and harassment, all of which need a developed record. The brief partly answers by alleging eight forums and a warning from the law director, but it still gives only a catalogue of filings and a conclusory accusation. On this record, this is the most serious weakness because the requested relief is an extraordinary sanctions/vexatious-litigant remedy.
challenges.suggested_response: R.C. 2323.52 addresses conduct, not merely the number of case captions in isolation. Here, Defendant showed that Appellant repeatedly filed actions and papers arising from the same dispute in multiple forums, continuing to pursue the same allegations against Appellee and others after being warned by the Cleveland Heights Law Director to stop harassing Appellee and to stay away. Appellant has identified no record showing a good-faith legal basis for that repetitive conduct. On this record, the trial court erred in denying sanctions and in declining to declare Appellant a vexatious litigator.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Make the sanction argument about the pattern of repeated, related filings and the alleged lack of any good-faith basis, not about the number of captions alone. If the record does not contain the underlying pleadings, acknowledge that the motion relied on the filings and the law-director warning already before the trial court.

challenges.opponent_argument: The summary-judgment argument cannot stand on the brief's repeated conclusion that the motion was "unopposed." Rule 56 still requires the movant to show no genuine issue of material fact, entitlement as a matter of law, and that reasonable minds can reach only one adverse conclusion when the evidence is viewed most strongly for the nonmovant. Temple, Delker, Mers, and Williams all state that standard; none says an unopposed motion is automatically entitled to judgment. challenges.judge_assessment: This lands. Ohio Civ.R. 56 still requires the movant to show no genuine issue of material fact and entitlement to judgment as a matter of law; a motion is not automatically granted just because it is unopposed. The brief does recite the Rule 56 standard and says the motion was well-taken, but it does not separately show why the record meets each requirement beyond conclusory assertions and a few factual statements. If the court accepts this attack, the summary-judgment affirmance is in real danger because the whole merits ruling depends on whether the Rule 56 record was actually carried.
challenges.suggested_response: The trial court did not grant summary judgment merely because Appellant failed to respond. The evidentiary materials before the court showed that Appellant was never legally married to the decedent, paid none of the funeral expenses, that the decedent’s mother paid the funeral bill in full, and that the cremains had already been buried. On that record, no genuine issue of material fact remained, and Appellee was entitled to judgment as a matter of law.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rely on the fact that the motion was unopposed. Add the actual record facts that support the Rule 56 ruling and state expressly why those facts left no genuine issue for trial.

The cited vexatious-litigator authority supports the need to tie repeated filings to the statutory elements, and the brief does rely heavily on a list of cases plus a brief assertion of harassment and bad faith. But the brief is not silent: it says appellant filed the matter in at least eight forums, continued filing related actions, and acted without a good-faith basis. challenges.suggested_response: Appellant’s filings were not isolated or unrelated. The record shows that he pursued the same cremains dispute in multiple courts, continued filing despite prior adverse proceedings, and did so after being warned to stop harassing Appellee. challenges.judge_assessment: On this record, this is the strongest attack. R.C. 5303.01 shows that recording a certified copy of a quiet-title judgment is a statutory recording step, but the brief does not cite authority showing that recording alone is the kind of 'execution' that moots appellate review. The authorities cited in the brief are generalized mootness/execution cases, mostly in possession or stay contexts, and the bridge from 'recorded judgment' to 'executed judgment' remains the weak link. The brief does answer by asserting that the judgment was executed before appeal and stay, but that is mostly a conclusion, not a sourced rule. If this point lands, Lender loses the threshold mootness dismissal.
challenges.suggested_response: On this record, the appeal was moot before the Stovalls sought any stay. Lender recorded a certified copy of the quiet-title judgment on August 13, 2024; the Stovalls did not appeal until the next day and did not move to stay until August 19. The trial court denied the stay as moot because Lender had already executed judgment, and the Eighth District dismissed the appeal for the same reason. The Stovalls cite no authority showing that this undisputed sequence leaves a live controversy for this Court to decide.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not rest the mootness argument on a bare statement that recording the certified judgment itself was "execution" unless you can add authority for that proposition. The safer response is to emphasize the undisputed chronology, the trial court’s own finding that the judgment had already been executed when the stay was sought, the Eighth District’s mootness dismissal, and the Stovalls’ concession that the judgment was satisfied.

attacks_proposed.argument: Appellee overstates the mootness rule by equating a certified-copy filing with "execution" of a quiet-title judgment. R.C. 5303.01 contemplates that the clerk will cause the judgment to be recorded in the deed records, which makes recording look like a statutory post-judgment ministerial step, not a separate enforcement event that automatically extinguishes appellate review. The authorities Appellee leans on address eviction-possession situations and stay-of-execution issues, not title-recordation under the quiet-title statute.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If recording is not the same thing as execution, the appeal is not moot on Appellee's theory and the Court cannot dismiss for lack of a live controversy.

attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: This undercuts Appellee's attempt to use waiver to insulate a shaky mootness ruling from review.

attacks_proposed.argument: Appellee is too quick to dismiss this as a routine Rule 56 dispute that can never qualify for review. The briefing itself centers on recurring legal questions about what counts as admissible summary-judgment evidence and what procedural protections apply in housing/title litigation. The authorities on affidavits, hearsay, and service show those are legal-rule questions, not just one-off factual disagreements.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the issue is framed as recurring legal doctrine rather than mere error correction, the public-interest/jurisdictional objection loses force.

attacks_proposed.argument: Appellee's due-process response proves too little. Saying the Stovalls "could have" filed discovery, briefs, and evidence does not establish that the process they actually received was constitutionally adequate; it only says they might have done more. The cited materials show that evidentiary and procedural rules matter in these cases, which is exactly why Appellee cannot convert a contested due-process claim into an insubstantial one by pointing to the appellants' litigation choices alone.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If due process is measured by meaningful opportunity and the handling of evidence, not by whether a party maximized every procedural option, the constitutional-question argument remains live.

attacks_proposed.argument: Appellee's merits fallback asks the Court to accept Appellee's own summary of the summary-judgment record, but no record has been supplied in this prompt to verify the claimed eight exhibits, sworn affidavits, or the asserted absence of rebuttal evidence. attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: Without an actual record basis, the Court should not accept Appellee's bare characterization of the evidence as a substitute for proof that summary judgment was proper.

The authorities cited in the brief are generalized mootness/execution cases, mostly in possession or stay contexts, and the bridge from 'recorded judgment' to 'executed judgment' remains the weak link. The brief does answer by asserting that the judgment was executed before appeal and stay, but that is mostly a conclusion, not a sourced rule. challenges.judge_assessment: This does not really answer the brief’s jurisdictional point. The listed grounds—abuse of discretion, lack of substantial evidence, inadmissible evidence, and denial of due process—are presented in the memorandum as case-specific error claims, not as propositions of law. O’Malley and Baughman support the brief’s distinction between settling law and settling cases, and the attack does not identify a discrete unsettled legal question that would pull the case into discretionary jurisdiction.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if the Court were to look past mootness, the Stovalls identify no unsettled question of law. Their listed "grounds" are labels for alleged error in this case—"abuse of discretion," "lack of substantial evidence," "reliance on inadmissible evidence," and "denial of due process"—not propositions of law requiring this Court’s resolution. Section 2, Article IV of the Ohio Constitution does not invite error correction; it authorizes this Court to settle the law, not to relitigate a summary-judgment order on a unique factual record. See State v. O’Malley, 2022-Ohio-3207, ¶ 50; Baughman v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 88 Ohio St.3d 480, 492 (2000) (Cook, J., concurring).
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the jurisdiction argument focused on the absence of any unsettled proposition of law. The filing should be characterized as a request to revisit case-specific summary-judgment rulings, which is not what this Court’s discretionary jurisdiction is for.

attacks_proposed.argument: Recording the certified judgment does not, by itself, establish mootness. Ohio authorities in the landlord-tenant/property context treat mootness as turning on whether the controversy has truly ended—such as a tenant’s voluntary vacatur—not merely on post-judgment enforcement steps. And Ohio title law recognizes that a deed need not be recorded to pass title, which undercuts the claim that recordation alone fully extinguished any live dispute or possible relief.
attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If recordation is not automatically mooting, the Court must confront the merits or at least the jurisdictional question instead of dismissing the appeal as purely academic.

attacks_proposed.argument: This is not fairly characterized as a mere routine Rule 56 dispute. attacks_proposed.whyItMatters: If the case presents a recurring title-and-possession question, the Court has a much stronger basis to treat it as legally significant rather than dismiss it as routine error correction.

results.assessment: The brief reads strongest on mootness, because it ties the dismissal to execution of the judgment and the absence of a stay, but it still makes a vulnerable leap from recording/execution to complete loss of live controversy, which the cited authorities do not squarely establish on their face. Its jurisdiction section is also thin: it treats the Stovalls’ filings as mere error correction, yet the challenge says the issues are substantive legal doctrines, so the brief needs a clearer explanation of why no unsettled question of law is actually presented. The due-process point is less exposed, though it should more directly address the difference between having a chance to litigate and constitutionally adequate procedure.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is a real pressure point because Westport itself says the SB 97 incorporation issue was the subject of a certified conflict and then pending in the Ohio Supreme Court. That does not make Westport's argument wrong on this record, but it does undercut any claim that the statute question was settled beyond dispute. The brief tries to answer it with Arn, Advent, and St. Clair, so the attack is not fatal; still, if the appellate court treats the conflict as unresolved and declines to extend those cases, Westport loses its statutory-no-coverage theory for the 2002 renewal.
challenges.suggested_response: Westport does not ask this Court to decide the broader conflict in the abstract; it asks the Court to apply the authorities it has cited, including Arn, Advent, and St. Clair, which hold that the law in effect at renewal governs and that UM/UIM coverage can no longer be implied by operation of law. The existence of a certified conflict does not create a genuine issue of material fact, and it does not prevent this Court from following the cases supporting application of the amended statute to the January 1, 2002 renewal. On this record, the trial court properly entered summary judgment because the policy in force on the date of loss renewed after S.B. 97 became effective.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Soften any claim that SB 97 was unquestionably settled law and instead say Westport relies on the appellate authorities it cites as controlling here. Acknowledge the certified-conflict posture only to say it does not create a factual dispute and does not prevent application of Arn, Advent, and St. Clair to the January 1, 2002 renewal.

challenges.judge_assessment: The brief does admit there was no separately printed policy for the December 1, 2000 to January 1, 2001 period and that a binder was used. The attack is that Westport never identifies the binder terms, so the court cannot assume the binder or later renewals settle the operative coverage language. That is a legitimate gap if plaintiffs are trying to make the binder period control. Westport's answer is that the later policies were produced and that no policy was withheld; if the court accepts the renewal-date analysis, the missing printed inception policy does not matter. If the court thinks the binder's contents could differ materially, Westport loses summary judgment.
challenges.suggested_response: Plaintiffs’ missing-policy argument fails because they identify no binder language showing UM/UIM coverage different from the later-produced policies. Westport’s evidence shows that the one-month inception coverage was evidenced by a binder and that the January 1, 2001 and January 1, 2002 policies were produced to plaintiffs. Under Civ.R. 56, speculation about what the binder might have said is not enough to create a genuine issue of material fact, and plaintiffs have not come forward with competent evidence of any different operative terms.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Answer the binder argument by emphasizing the absence of any competent evidence of different binder language, not by implying the binder’s contents. The brief should say plaintiffs have not produced or identified binder terms that create coverage, so speculation about what the binder might have said cannot defeat summary judgment.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is essentially the same fight as Westport's renewal-date theory. The brief does not just assert the January 1, 2002 renewal; it also says the policy chain began on December 1, 2000, that SB 267 was already in force when the coverage was first written, and that SB 97 was incorporated at the next renewal. So the brief does answer the continuity point. The advocate still stands to lose if the court reads Wolfe and the renewal statutes to mean the original inception date, not the renewal date, controls the UM/UIM issue. But as written, Westport has a nonfrivolous answer and the attack is not an obvious factual knockout.
challenges.suggested_response: The continuous chain of coverage does not help plaintiffs. Westport’s evidence shows that S.B. 267 was already in effect when the coverage was first written in December 2000, and that S.B. 97 became effective before the January 1, 2002 renewal. Under the authorities Westport cites, the law in effect at renewal governs the policy in force on the date of loss, so UM/UIM coverage could not be implied as a matter of law on July 15, 2002.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the continuous-coverage facts but convert them into a renewed-policy answer: the continuous chain does not help plaintiffs because SB 267 was already in force at inception and SB 97 was in force before the January 1, 2002 renewal. challenges.opponent_argument: The statute text Westport quotes does not itself resolve the renewal question in Westport's favor; it only says a policy that falls within the statute 'may, but is not required to' include UM/UIM coverage. Westport still must establish that the policy in force on the loss date is the controlling policy for this analysis and that the statutory amendment properly reaches it. The brief assumes that step instead of proving it.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the amendment's application to this policy chain is not established, Westport's no-implied-coverage argument falls away.

results.assessment: The brief has real strength where it ties the policies to Pennsylvania/Florida vehicles, the out-of-Ohio issuance, and the January 1, 2002 renewal after S.B. 97, and its treatment of the excess policy is serviceable on this record. Its biggest weakness is that it leans hard on a statutory theory Westport itself admits was the subject of a certified conflict, so the court can treat the no-coverage rule as unsettled rather than settled. It also leaves a genuine opening on the missing inception binder because it never identifies the binder’s terms, which is the cleanest attack on the continuity theory. The renewal-date framing is plausible, but not yet airtight.

challenges.opponent_argument: The Commercial Excess Policy argument is conclusory. Westport says the excess policy cannot create UM/UIM coverage because the underlying policies do not provide it, but the brief identifies no policy language in the excess layer that eliminates UM/UIM coverage on its own. The fact that the policy is excess or umbrella coverage (u24) does not, by itself, answer whether its own terms provide a separate grant of coverage.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the excess policy has independent coverage language, summary judgment cannot be affirmed on a blanket assumption that the absence of UM/UIM in the primary layer automatically defeats the excess layer.

target.excerpt: 3) The Commercial Excess Policy is not required to provide UM/UIM coverage where there is no such coverage under the underlying Auto and General Liability policies.

challenges.judge_assessment: This is the strongest attack. Westport's excess-policy point is stated as a conclusion, not as a rule tied to policy text or cited authority. On this record, the brief says only that the Commercial Excess Policy sits above primary insurance and follows the underlying structure; it does not quote a provision saying UM/UIM is excluded or that the excess layer cannot stand alone. An Ohio court could therefore treat the excess-policy theory as underdeveloped if the appellants can point to independent excess coverage language. Westport stands to lose the excess-policy affirmance if the policy is not purely follow-form or if it is itself within the statute.
challenges.suggested_response: The Commercial Excess Policy does not independently create UM/UIM coverage. The record describes it as providing sums in excess of primary insurance that the insured becomes obligated to pay, and sums in excess of a retained limit for certain injuries for which primary insurance coverage is not afforded; it is also subject to the same terms, conditions, exclusions, definitions and limitations as the primary insurance. Appellants identify no provision in Exhibit 5 granting separate UM/UIM coverage, and no authority requiring such coverage to be implied in the excess layer.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: The excess-policy argument needs to be made from the policy language already in the record, not as a bare conclusion. Use the description in the brief that the excess policy provides only sums in excess of primary insurance and retained limits, and say appellants identify no separate UM/UIM grant in Exhibit 5.

challenges.opponent_argument: Westport's threshold R.C. 3937.18 argument is too broad because its own facts say the Business Auto Policy provided $50,000 in UM/UIM coverage for "owned autos only" and included Pennsylvania and Florida UM/UIM forms (u40). That means the real issue is not simply whether the statute applies, but what the policy itself says. The brief does not eliminate the possibility of express contractual UM/UIM coverage; it only argues against coverage implied by law.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the policy already contains some UM/UIM language, Westport cannot win by stopping at statutory inapplicability. The court would still need to interpret the contract language, which the brief does not do.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack has some traction only if plaintiffs are actually claiming express UM/UIM coverage under the policy text rather than solely implied coverage by operation of law. The brief's statutory-applicability section does not fully analyze the contractual UM/UIM language; it mainly argues that Ohio's statute does not apply and therefore no coverage is implied. That said, the brief does say the policy had Pennsylvania and Florida UM/UIM forms and no Ohio endorsement, which substantially answers the point to the extent the claim is about Ohio-implied coverage. On this record, the court is unlikely to reverse on this attack alone unless the policy text shows a separate Ohio contractual grant of coverage.
challenges.suggested_response: The issue is whether Ohio law compels UM/UIM coverage to be implied into these policies by operation of law. It does not. The Business Auto Policy contains Pennsylvania and Florida UM/UIM forms, not an Ohio UM endorsement, and Press was driving his own vehicle, not a covered auto. To the extent the policy affords limited UM/UIM protection under other states’ forms for owned autos, that does not create Ohio-imposed coverage for this loss. Appellants identify no Ohio contractual grant of UM/UIM coverage applicable here.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Narrow this point to implied coverage by operation of law and make clear that appellants have identified no Ohio contractual grant that would extend to Press’s loss. The brief can rely on the policy facts already in the record: the Business Auto Policy contains Pennsylvania and Florida UM/UIM forms, no Ohio UM endorsement, and Press was driving his own vehicle rather than a covered auto.

challenges.opponent_argument: The SB 97 renewal theory is not a clean basis for summary judgment because Westport itself admits the controlling appellate law is split and the question is pending before the Ohio Supreme Court (u95). A party cannot ask for affirmance on the premise that the law is settled in its favor when its own brief concedes the exact issue is unresolved between Advent and Storer.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the renewal rule is unsettled, Westport has not shown that SB 97 unquestionably governs the January 1, 2002 renewal, so the judgment cannot rest on that ground alone.

target.excerpt: B. SUMMARY JUDGMENT WAS PROPERLY GRANTED IN FAVOR OF APPELLEE WHERE SENATE BILL 97 GOVERNS THE WESTPORT POLICIES AND UM/UIM COVERAGE CAN NO LONGER BE IMPLIED AS A MATTER OF LAW.

challenges.judge_assessment: The conflict between Advent and Storer does not defeat Westport's position on this record. The brief already acknowledges the split, quotes the conflicting line of cases, and argues why the January 1, 2002 renewal falls on the Arn/Advent side. An appellate court can still choose the rule it finds more persuasive; the existence of a certified conflict means the issue is unsettled, not that Westport necessarily loses. This attack weakens the SB 97 ground, but it does not knock out the judgment because Westport also relies on statutory inapplicability.
challenges.suggested_response: Even if the Court reaches the Senate Bill 97 issue, the better-reasoned authority is Arn and Advent. Under those cases, the law in effect at the renewal governs the scope of UM/UIM coverage, and Westport’s January 1, 2002 renewal occurred after SB 97 became effective on October 31, 2001. Accordingly, the trial court correctly held that UM/UIM coverage could not be implied by operation of law under the renewal policy at issue.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Do not argue that the law is settled in Westport’s favor. Instead, say that even if the Court reaches the SB 97 issue, the better line of authority is Arn and Advent, and the January 1, 2002 renewal is the operative policy period.

challenges.opponent_argument: Westport's statutory-applicability theory depends on disputed factual predicates that the brief treats as established without a record showing they are undisputed: where delivery occurred, what the operative policy period was, and whether the vehicle-garaging facts are complete for the policies at issue (u39-u40). Those are not mere labels; they are the facts that trigger or defeat R.C. 3937.18. Without a record demonstrating them, the court should not affirm summary judgment on Westport's say-so.
challenges.why_it_matters: If the factual predicates for inapplicability are not conclusively established, the court cannot hold that R.C. 3937.18 is out of the case as a matter of law.

challenges.judge_assessment: The brief supplies specific record facts supporting delivery, garaging, and policy location: the policies were issued from Kansas to a Pennsylvania insured, the covered vehicles were garaged in Florida and Pennsylvania, and no Ohio UM endorsement appears. The attack is therefore more a challenge to the sufficiency of the evidentiary record than to the legal rule. On the brief's present record, an Ohio court would likely find the statutory-applicability issue properly framed for summary judgment unless appellants produced contrary evidence.
challenges.suggested_response: The facts supporting non-applicability are undisputed on this record. The Business Auto and Commercial Excess Policies were issued from Kansas to PS Management in Pennsylvania, the scheduled autos were garaged in Florida and Pennsylvania, and the Business Auto Policy contains no Ohio UM endorsement. On those facts, Ohio Revised Code Section 3937.18 does not apply, and Appellants identified no contrary evidence creating a genuine issue of material fact.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the statutory-applicability argument anchored in the record facts and the absence of contrary evidence. State the delivery, garaging, and endorsement facts as undisputed summary-judgment facts, not as assumptions.

challenges.opponent_argument: Arn v. McLean does not fully support Westport's position. The brief's own description of Arn involves a February 21, 2002 renewal after S.B. 97 had already become effective (u74-u77). Westport never explains why that posture controls a policy sequence that began with a December 1, 2000 bind and a January 1, 2001 renewal, especially in light of the contrary Storer rule it also cites (u91).
challenges.why_it_matters: Removing Arn as a clean fit weakens Westport's main authority for applying S.B. 97 at renewal and undercuts the claim that UM/UIM could not be implied as a matter of law.

target.excerpt: In Arn, the insured was involved in an automobile accident on July 12, 2002. Her automobile coverage through State Farm had most recently renewed on February 21, 2002. Id. at PP 6, 16. State Farm maintained that its obligation with regard to UM/UIM coverage was determined by Ohio Revised Code Sectio

challenges.judge_assessment: Arn is not a clean fit only if one ignores the brief's own chronology. Westport uses Arn for the proposition that the law at a renewal governs UM/UIM obligations, and its facts here are the same type of timing problem: a renewal after SB 97 became effective. The attack is right that the brief does not fully reconcile Arn with Storer, but the brief already tries to do that by distinguishing the cases and citing Advent and St. Clair. That makes this a debatable authority-point, not a serious defect on this record.
challenges.suggested_response: Arn remains persuasive because it turns on the law in effect at renewal, not the date the policy relationship first began. Here, as in Arn, the operative renewal occurred after SB 97 became effective, so the amended statute governed the January 1, 2002 policy period. Storer is distinguishable because, unlike this case, the brief shows that SB 267 was already in effect when the coverage was first written and that SB 97 became effective before the January 1, 2002 renewal.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Tighten the Arn discussion to the point that matters: the law at renewal controls. Emphasize that Westport’s January 1, 2002 renewal came after SB 97 was effective, and distinguish Storer on the timing Westport already identified in the brief.

The main weakness is the Commercial Excess Policy argument, which reads as a conclusion rather than a text-based explanation of why that layer cannot independently supply UM/UIM coverage. challenges.judge_assessment: This lands hard. The brief tries to satisfy Scholler by saying Solomon had 'privity of contract' with Harwood and by relying on concurrency, but that is not the same as privity with Horvath's client in the attorney-malpractice sense. The brief also leans on malice, but if the court rejects the privity theory, the claim still needs the narrow malice exception. On this record, Horvath has a strong path to affirmance unless Solomon can show a recognized third-party duty or true malicious conduct.
challenges.suggested_response: Horvath is not liable merely because Solomon had a contract with Harwood; the malpractice claim survives because Scholler also permits a nonclient claim where the attorney acts maliciously. Here, the record, viewed in Solomon's favor, permits an inference that Horvath knowingly concealed the Mustafa transaction, assured counsel that Harwood would close with Solomon, and then attempted to terminate Solomon's contract so Harwood could proceed with the alternate sale. Those facts, if believed, support a finding that Horvath acted with conscious disregard for Solomon's rights, making summary judgment improper on the malice issue.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Drop the privity theory unless the brief can cite a real attorney-client or third-party-duty authority that is not in the current record. The safer path is to rely on Scholler's malicious-conduct exception and to present malice as a fact question.

challenges.judge_assessment: This attack has some force, but it is not fatal on the face of the brief because Solomon does cite evidence that Gill had funds available if loan conditions were met and that the seller cut off the transaction before closing. The real weakness is that the brief is trying to turn a disputed financing record into a certainty. On summary judgment, though, the court is supposed to view conflicts in Solomon's favor, so this is more of a close factual issue than a clean defeat.
challenges.suggested_response: At summary judgment, Solomon was not required to prove conclusively that the transaction would have closed; he was required only to show a genuine dispute of material fact. Gill's affidavit states that he had the funds available to close before the end of the day on December 14, 2007, if the loan conditions were met, and the contemporaneous communications show that Gill, Lynch, and Solomon were still working toward closing when Harwood, through Horvath, terminated the transaction on December 13, 2007. Viewing that evidence most strongly in Solomon's favor, a reasonable trier of fact could conclude that Solomon was ready, willing, and able to perform and that Harwood's repudiation caused the failure to close.
challenges.coaching_recommendation: Keep the argument framed as a genuine-issue-of-material-fact point, not as a conclusive statement that Solomon definitely could have closed. The brief should rely on Gill's affidavit and the December 13 communications to show conflicting evidence under Civ.R. 56.

As framed, the argument tries to use unclean hands to knock out summary judgment across contract, negligence, malpractice, and damages issues, which is a much broader use than the cited doctrine plainly supports. Harwood, Resource, and Horvath do not come to this Court with clean hands: the record describes a false HUD-1, concealment of the Mustafa transaction, and conduct directed toward defeating Solomon's contractual and equitable rights.
